title: A Simple Pause Between Tasks
markdown:
# A Simple Pause Between Tasks

Many people who want to reflect more regularly find that long journaling sessions or twenty-minute meditations are hard to keep up. The intention is good, but the practice competes with work, meals, errands, and sleep. A smaller approach is to use transitions you already make: the moment between finishing one task and starting the next. This pause does not require a notebook, a timer, or a quiet room. It asks only that you notice what is happening as one activity ends and another begins.

Impermanence is the idea that nothing stays the same, including your mood, your energy, and the situation in front of you. A pause between tasks is a way to meet that fact directly. Instead of treating your day as one continuous block, you notice where one thing ends and another begins. This does not require you to believe anything or adopt a new identity. It only asks you to pay attention to a moment that already exists.

## The Practice: A Pause Between Tasks

1. Pick one transition. Choose a shift you will make today, such as ending a work block and preparing a meal, or finishing a phone call and opening your email.
2. Stop for thirty seconds. When you reach the end of the first task, pause before you begin the second. You can stand or sit where you are. You do not need to close your eyes.
3. Notice three things. Feel your feet on the floor or your body in the chair. Notice the pace of your breath without trying to change it. Listen for one sound nearby, such as traffic, an appliance, or a voice in another room.
4. Name the shift. Silently say what just ended and what is starting, for example, "I am done answering messages. I am beginning to make lunch." Do not judge whether the first task went well or poorly.
5. Resume. Move to the next task when you are ready.

The whole sequence takes less than a minute. You can repeat it once a day or at several transitions if it feels useful. There is no correct number of times to do it.

## What to Notice During the Pause

The goal is not to clear your mind or force yourself to feel calm. It is to create a short gap where you register change instead of sliding from one activity to the next without noticing.

Here is an example. Maya works from home. She usually moves straight from her laptop to cooking dinner, often while still thinking about an email she just sent. Today she tries the pause. She closes her laptop, stands in the kitchen, and feels her feet against the floor. She hears the refrigerator hum. She notes that her shoulders feel tight. She tells herself, "Work time is ending. Dinner time is starting." She does not try to relax her shoulders; she simply acknowledges them. Then she starts chopping vegetables.

Later she realizes she noticed the tight shoulders before they became a headache. That was not the goal of the exercise, but it happened because she stopped long enough to feel what was already there.

Your example might look different. You might notice the weight of a mug, the sound of traffic outside, or the fact that you are holding your breath. Any observation counts. The exercise is useful when you observe without trying to fix anything.

## Making It Fit Your Day

You do not need to do this at the same time every day. Pick transitions that already exist in your routine so you do not have to remember a new habit from scratch.

Some useful moments include ending a meeting and checking messages, parking the car and entering a building, or putting down a book and turning off the light. If you work in an office, you might pause before you log in each morning or before you leave your desk at the end of the day. If you care for children, you might pause between helping with homework and starting bedtime. The specific transition matters less than the act of stopping.

If you forget, simply start again at the next transition. There is no streak to protect and no score to keep.

If thirty seconds feels too long, try ten seconds. If naming the shift feels awkward, skip the words and only notice the physical sensations. You can also tie the pause to an object you already touch, such as a door handle or a kettle, so the object reminds you to stop.

Over time, you may notice transitions more often without planning to. You might catch yourself before you speak sharply, or before you reach for your phone the moment you sit down. These moments may or may not happen, and they are not the measure of whether the practice is useful. The practice is the pause itself.
